subject: Anthropology
title: Oldowan Tools
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Oldowan Tools.

hook.text: Strike one rock against another at the right angle. A sharp flake chips off. Technology is born.

buildup.text: Oldowan tools are the oldest known stone tools, dating to about 2.6 million years ago in East Africa.

discovery.text: Simple choppers and flakes were used to cut meat, scrape hides, and crack bones for energy-rich marrow.

twist.text: Making them required planning and skill. The toolmaker had to choose the right rock and strike precisely.

climax.text: Oldowan tools mark the moment hominins began shaping the world instead of just living in it.

punchline.text: One sharp edge started two million years of innovation.

quiz.question: What were Oldowan tools primarily used for?

details.summary: Oldowan tools are the oldest established stone tool tradition, dating from about 2.6 million years ago. They consist of simple flakes struck from cores — basic but effective for cutting, scraping, and processing food. They represent the technological starting point of human material culture.
details.whyItMatters: Oldowan tools mark the beginning of a continuous technological tradition that leads directly to modern technology. These simple flakes initiated the ratchet of cumulative culture that would eventually produce agriculture, writing, and computers.
takeaways: Oldowan tools date from about 2.6 million years ago
They are simple flakes struck from stone cores
They represent the starting point of cumulative material culture

faq.question: What could Oldowan tools be used for?
faq.answer: Despite their simplicity, Oldowan flakes are sharp enough to cut meat, scrape hides, process plant foods, and sharpen wooden tools. Experimental archaeology shows they are surprisingly effective for basic tasks. Their simplicity belies their functional versatility and cognitive significance.

faq.question: How were Oldowan tools made?
faq.answer: By striking a stone core with a hammerstone to detach sharp flakes. This requires understanding stone fracture mechanics, selecting appropriate raw materials, and controlling the angle and force of strikes. Even this basic technology involves cognitive abilities beyond any non-human primate.
